summary: Describes the User-based Security Model for SNMP version 3, which provides message-level security, defining procedures for authentication and privacy. It also includes a MIB for remotely managing the model's configuration. It was replaced by RFC 2274.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives each network-manager message a signature and an optional seal, so only the right people can send and read them.

questions: what is the snmpv3 user-based security model
what is replay protection in snmp
subtitle: Authenticating and encrypting SNMPv3 messages with user identities, keys, and replay protection.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 needs to prove the identity of the sender, ensure messages have not been altered, and optionally hide message contents, without relying on external services like NTP or PKI key management.
tldr.mechanism: Each SNMP user has an identity, authentication key (for HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA), and optionally a privacy key (for DES encryption). Messages include engine ID, boot count, and timestamp to prevent replay attacks. The receiving engine verifies the authentication digest and checks that the message timestamp is recent and from the intended engine.
tldr.outcome: SNMP messages can be sent over untrusted networks with assurance that they came from an authorized user, have not been altered in transit, and were not previously sent or sent to the wrong destination. RFC 2274 replaced this model with updated authentication and privacy algorithms.

today: RFC 2264 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 2274, which replaced HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 with HMAC-SHA-96 and HMAC-SHA-224/256, and replaced CBC-DES with AES in CFB mode for better security. USM remains the standard authentication and privacy framework for SNMPv3.

sections.title: Message-Level Security for SNMPv3
sections.content:
Network management requires two different kinds of security. First, messages must be authenticated: the receiver must be certain the message came from the claimed sender and was not altered in transit. Second, privacy may be needed: sensitive management information should not be visible to eavesdroppers on the network. The User-based Security Model (USM) provides both, working alongside SNMPv3's access control to ensure only authorized users can read and modify management data.

USM is self-contained: it does not depend on external services like NTP for time synchronization or certificate authorities for key management. Instead, each SNMP engine manages its own users and secrets, and time is tracked locally using boot count and elapsed seconds. This design makes SNMP deployable in isolated networks and simplifies initial configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: USM is like signing a letter with your secret signature, adding the date and your address, so the receiver knows the letter came from you, wasn't changed in the mail, and isn't an old copy you sent before.

sections.title: Users, Keys, and Authentication
sections.content:
The core concept of USM is a user, identified by a userName and securityName. Each user has two secrets: an authKey for authenticating messages, and optionally a privKey for encrypting them. The user also specifies which authentication protocol (HMAC-MD5-96 or HMAC-SHA-96) and privacy protocol (CBC-DES) to use.

When sending a message, the security model computes an authentication digest (a keyed hash) over the entire message using the user's authKey. The receiver recomputes the digest using its copy of the authKey and compares it to the received digest. If they match, the message is authentic and has not been altered. If privacy is enabled, the message payload (the scopedPDU) is encrypted using the user's privKey before transmission.

Keys are not transmitted over the network. Instead, they are pre-shared or installed through out-of-band means. The RFC includes algorithms for deriving keys from passphrases, but the actual key material stays local to each SNMP engine.
sections.plainLanguage: A user is like a person with a password. To sign a message, you use the password to create a checksum that proves you sent it. To hide a message, you scramble it with the password. The person on the other end uses their copy of the password to unsign and unscramble.

sections.title: Replay Protection and Time Windows
sections.content:
Simply authenticating a message is not enough if an attacker can capture and replay old authentic messages. USM prevents replay through three mechanisms that are always transmitted with an authenticated message.

First, the msgAuthoritativeEngineID uniquely identifies the sender or intended recipient of the message. If an attacker replays a message to the wrong engine, the receiving engine detects the mismatch and rejects it.

Second, msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots and msgAuthoritativeEngineTime record the authoritative engine's boot count and seconds since boot. When the authoritative engine reboots, the boot counter increments and time resets. The receiving engine checks these values are within a time window (150 seconds by default) of its own estimate of the sender's time. Messages outside this window—either too old or impossibly far in the future—are rejected.

Third, non-authoritative engines (clients) synchronize their clock estimate with the authoritative engine (the server) by reading the time values from authentic incoming messages. They cache the latest time value they have seen and compare incoming messages against it, ensuring even rapid replays within the same second are caught.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a signed message, you write down: who you are, how many times you've restarted, and how many seconds have passed since restart. If someone tries to replay your message to someone else, the address is wrong. If they try to replay an old message, the time is wrong. If they try to send two messages so quickly the time hasn't advanced, that's caught too.

sections.title: Authentication Protocols: HMAC-MD5 and HMAC-SHA
sections.content:
USM defines two authentication protocols, both based on keyed hash functions.

HMAC-MD5-96 computes an HMAC (Hashed Message Authentication Code) using the MD5 hash function and the user's authKey. The first 96 bits (12 bytes) of the resulting digest are used in the message. MD5 produces a 128-bit hash, and truncating to 96 bits balances computational cost with collision resistance.

HMAC-SHA-96 uses the SHA-1 hash function instead, computing an HMAC over the entire message and truncating the result to 96 bits. SHA-1 is considered more conservative cryptographically than MD5 and is the RECOMMENDED authentication protocol.

Both protocols require that the authentication happen first: if both authentication and privacy are enabled, the complete message (including encrypted payload) is authenticated. This ensures an attacker cannot decrypt and reencrypt a message under a different user without detection.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign a message, you mix your password with the message through a mathematical process that always produces the same 12-byte signature for the same password and message. MD5 and SHA are two different mathematical recipes. SHA is considered safer, but both work.

sections.title: Privacy: CBC-DES Encryption
sections.content:
USM defines one privacy protocol: CBC-DES (Cipher Block Chaining with Data Encryption Standard). When privacy is requested, only the message payload (the scopedPDU) is encrypted; the header and authentication information remain in plaintext so the message can be routed and authenticated.

DES uses a 56-bit key (packed into 8 bytes with parity bits) and divides the payload into 8-byte blocks. CBC mode chains the blocks so that encrypting the same plaintext with the same key produces different ciphertext each time due to the random initialization vector. The sender generates a random IV and sends it with the encrypted data; the receiver uses the IV to decrypt.

A user's privKey is localized to each SNMP engine where the user is known, similar to authKey localization. This way, the user can have different privacy keys at different engines without creating a single point of failure or requiring a secure central key server.
sections.plainLanguage: To hide a message, you scramble it block by block using your password and a random starting point. The receiver needs the same password and starting point to unscramble. DES is the scrambling algorithm; CBC is the method of chaining blocks together.

sections.title: Key Localization and Configuration
sections.content:
One subtlety of USM is that the same user can exist on multiple SNMP engines with different keys at each engine. The user 'alice' might have one authKey at the monitoring station and a different authKey at each managed device. This key localization is handled through a combination of the user's securityName (a device-independent identifier) and the engine's snmpEngineID (which uniquely identifies each SNMP engine). The system can thus avoid a single master password and instead require secure out-of-band configuration or initial bootstrap of keys at each location.

When a non-authoritative engine (client) first contacts an authoritative engine (server), it performs discovery to learn the server's snmpEngineID. It then requests the server's time values and caches them, performing time synchronization. Once synchronized, the client can send properly authenticated requests. The RFC includes recommended initial configuration parameters and a password-to-key algorithm for deriving keys from passphrases, allowing administrators to configure users more easily while still protecting against dictionary attacks through key length (at least 16 bytes for MD5).
sections.plainLanguage: Alice has different passwords at different devices, so if someone learns her password at one place, they can't use it everywhere else. When Alice first contacts a new device, she learns its clock and then can send properly signed messages.

viz.caption: USM security parameters in SNMPv3 message

fields.name: Authoritative Engine ID
fields.desc: Identifies the SNMP engine (sender for response, receiver for request)

fields.name: Engine Boots
fields.desc: Number of times the authoritative engine has rebooted

fields.name: Engine Time
fields.desc: Seconds since last reboot at the authoritative engine

fields.name: User Name
fields.desc: User on whose behalf message is sent

fields.name: Authentication Parameters
fields.desc: HMAC digest (first 96 bits); empty if noAuth

fields.name: Privacy Parameters
fields.desc: IV for DES; empty if noPriv
